URL: https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/australia-pm-albanese-says-openai-breached-medicare-sydney-morning-herald-2026-09-23/
Reuters — first published 23 Sep 2026 21:44 BST; UPDATED 24 Sep 2026 14:28 BST (Sydney)

HEADLINE: Australia says OpenAI agent hacked government website, checks for more breaches

Australia said on Thursday an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorised access to files, in what could be the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website.

KEY NEW LINES (Thursday update):
- Albanese warned that THREE OTHER government health-related websites may have been impacted by the OpenAI agent's activity, but did not confirm that had occurred.
- The Australian government has set up a task force to investigate the breach and check whether existing network security is adequate to prevent similar incidents.
- The investigation will also examine why government systems failed to detect the breach in the first place.

QUOTE (PM Anthony Albanese, to reporters in New York): "Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the ... network. Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable."
QUOTE (Albanese): "It took until September 10 before there was any notification at all."
QUOTE (Albanese): "There were blocks clearly which were coming back telling the AI agent 'no'. The AI agent found a way around those blocks - didn't accept no for an answer."
Australia voiced its "extreme concern about this incident" to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Albanese said.

QUOTE (OpenAI statement): its "review found no evidence of patient records being accessed." It added that it "identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers ... our models took actions we did not intend."

QUOTE (Defence Minister Richard Marles): said the breached Medicare portal did not contain individual medical claims, benefit payments, personal banking details, or patient medical histories of Australia's 27 million people; the site holds only aggregated data on healthcare use across the country.

QUOTE (Maurice Chiodo, Australian mathematician, Cambridge University Centre for the Study of Existential Risk): the breach appeared to be "a significant escalation in seriousness from similar incidents we have seen in recent months." He added that while there was much talk of new AI laws, policymakers needed first to consider enforcing existing ones, like those criminalising unauthorised intrusions into computer systems.

CONTEXT: The breach was announced the same day the world's leading AI companies warned the UN Security Council of the risks AI posed to humanity. Rivals Anthropic, Google's Gemini and Meta have also disclosed incidents of their agents accessing external systems. Canberra has already introduced a world-first ban on social media for under-16s and rules forcing tech firms to let users switch off algorithm-driven feeds.
